context: Current closing price of Berkshire Hathaway B (BRK-B): $511.60 USD as of 2026-08-03.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a modestly bullish near-term bias anchored around the prevailing price level of the S&P 500 ETF (SPY) at the time of the forecast, which was trading in the low 510s. For the one-day horizon, I expected minimal drift from the last close, so the 512.5 estimate was essentially a slight upward nudge from current levels, consistent with the historical tendency for small positive daily returns on average. For the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 514, reflecting that over short multi-day windows the index tends to drift upward in the absence of major catalysts, though the edge is small. The one-month estimate of 518 continued that same logic, extrapolating a modest positive drift consistent with long-run average monthly equity returns of roughly 0.5–1%.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility of SPY at each horizon. Daily SPY moves have a standard deviation of roughly 1–1.5%, which translates to a roughly ±10 point range for a 90% interval at the one-day horizon. As the horizon extended to one week, I scaled uncertainty by the square root of time, roughly doubling the daily range to produce the ±20 point band. For one month, uncertainty widened further to roughly ±40 points, reflecting both the accumulation of daily volatility and the increased probability of regime-changing macro events over a longer window.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise Federal Reserve policy shift, a significant deterioration in labor market data, an escalation in geopolitical conflict, or renewed stress in the banking or credit system could easily drive SPY down 5–10% or more within a month. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, a dovish pivot signal from the Fed, or a resolution of trade or geopolitical tensions could propel prices meaningfully above the upper bound. Liquidity events or flash crashes, while rare, represent tail risks that conventional volatility scaling underestimates, meaning the true tails of the distribution are likely fatter than my stated intervals imply.
